title: Bridgewell Dedicated Readiness & Burst Playbook

Agreed next steps: send sizing spreadsheet, request sample traces, propose PoC plan and schedule SE benchmark session.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE); Malik Chen (Redwood SE); Aisha Kapoor (Bridgewell Head of ML); Tom Reynolds (Bridgewell Platform Eng); Maria Santos (Bridgewell SecOps); Ben Harper (Product, joined late)

Summary (auto): kickoff discovery around dedicated/reserved GPUs, isolation needs, burst strategy and security/compliance handshake.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for joining. uh quick intros? we can run 45 minutes or so and leave time for Qs. our goal is just to understand your traffic patterns and constraints and then recommend reserved sizing and a PoC approach.
[00:18] Aisha (Bridgewell): Hi — Aisha here. We're looking to replace parts of our customer-facing inference backend, right now it's a mix of hosted API calls and internal inference clusters. Latency matters for chat experiences.
[00:30] Tom (Bridgewell): Tom — platform. we run on AWS, mostly EKS, some onprem for a few regulated customers. big question for us is isolation — multi-tenant vs single-tenant. cost vs latenty tradeoffs.
[00:42] Maria (Bridgewell): Maria — security. SOC2 in flight, strong preference for KMS + audit logs, need SAML/Okta SSO and RBAC. also asking about data residency options.
[00:55] Malik (Redwood-SE): thanks. quick clarifying Q: when you say "hosted API calls", is that external third-party models? or your own model hosted internally?
[01:05] Aisha: it's a mix. some calls go to public LLM APIs for rapid prototyping; critical traffic we run on our in-house fine-tuned models. moving toward a dedicated pool for production inference to lower jitter and costs.
[01:18] Jordan: perfect. we'll walk through a few patterns — hosted, dedicated, private — but we'll focus on dedicated reserved GPU sizing and burst strategy since that's what you flagged.

[02:05] Malik: can you describe the current 95th/99th latency expectations?
[02:09] Tom: target is sub-300ms p95 for short-turn chat (<=512 tokens) and p99 under 700ms, for image-captioning stuff we're looser. during big launches our qps can jump 6x for 5-10 minutes.
[02:25] Aisha: we're seeing hourly peaks and sometimes daily sharp spikes when marketing pushes new features.

[03:00] Jordan: ok noted. typical dedicated patterns we recommend: reserved baseline for sustained qps + warm pool (prewarmed nodes) to handle spike absorb, then autoscale or burst to shared nodes or a less expensive quantized model var.
[03:20] Tom: how does warm pool work practically? like how many seconds to spin up?
[03:24] Malik: good question — warm pool keeps pre-initialized model state so new containers can accept requests in ~200-800ms depending on model and sequence length. cold start to a GPU could be multiple seconds to tens of seconds if loading big weights. warmpool/warmpool spelling — sorry. transcription note.
[03:45] Maria: and what about tenant fencing? we have regulated customers that require logical separation and distinct audit trails.
[03:52] Malik: we support tenant fencing via dedicated pools per customer or strict namespace isolation on dedicated clusters with network policies and separate log sinks. for highest isolation we recommend dedicated capacity per tenant.

[05:10] Aisha: budget guidance — if we reserve capacity what kind of utilization should we assume to be cost-effective?
[05:17] Jordan: generally aim for 60–80% steady utilization. reserved capacity makes sense when you have predictable baseline traffic. For unpredictable bursts, combine a smaller reserved baseline + warmpool + burst fallback to shared or lower-cost quantized models.
[05:35] Tom: do you provide quantized model variants automatically? we often need 4-bit runs for cost reasons.
[05:39] Malik: yes, we can serve quantized variants and recommend quantization level based on your model family and quality targets. we also track quality regressions with eval sets.

[07:00] Aisha: networking — we have strict VPC peering and enforced egress rules. can Redwood Dedicated live inside our VPC?
[07:08] Jordan: yes for Private we can install a control plane with VPC integration; Dedicated has options for VPC peering and private networking. details depend on whether you need on-prem air-gapped or managed VPC.
[07:25] Maria: KMS — do you integrate with our AWS KMS or do you require bringing keys?
[07:30] Malik: we support customer-managed KMS and can integrate with AWS KMS, HSMs for private deployments, and we persist audit logs to your log sinks.

[09:12] Ben (Bridgewell, late): sorry — jumped on, quick Q on SLA. we need a contractual uptime and tail latency SLA for paid customers. what's typical?
[09:20] Jordan: for Dedicated we commit to an availability SLA (we can propose 99.9% for reserved pools) and latency SLOs with clear remediation. for enterprise Private we can negotiate stricter terms.

[10:05] Tom: curious about per-token pricing when reserved vs on-demand — how do we model that?
[10:12] Jordan: reserved amortizes infra cost over committed units — we give a reserved GPU rate + lower per-token execution cost for baseline traffic, and then overage/burst pricing for additional capacity. I'll send a spreadsheet that models utilization scenarios.

[11:40] Malik: a couple more technicals — do you do KV cache sharing across requests for chat? because chat-heavy workloads benefit from KV cache locality.
[11:49] Aisha: yes we use KV cache per session. we want your runtime to be efficient so we don't double memory copy on handoffs.
[12:00] Malik: our runtime supports per-session KV caching with GPU-resident caches; we can route sticky sessions to the same warm node or use distributed KV with small network penalty. the strategy depends on session stickiness.

[13:30] Jordan: can you share numbers — baseline qps, burst qps, average tokens per request?
[13:35] Tom: baseline ~120 qps, average tokens about 220 per request, bursts up to 720 qps for short windows (5–12 minutes). auth traffic smaller but control plane heavy.
[13:55] Aisha: also some long context requests up to 2k tokens but rare — maybe 0.5% of traffic.

[15:05] Malik: that profile suggests a reserved baseline sized for ~150 qps to be safe, with a warm pool sized at ~8–12 GPUs to absorb spike delta and a burst plan to fall back to quantized instances for elastic capacity.
[15:25] Tom: would you recommend segregating regulated tenants on separate cards or can we do vGPU-level isolation?
[15:32] Malik: for strict compliance, separate dedicated pools is simplest; vGPU or tenant fencing can work but increases complexity and blast radius.

[17:00] Maria: audits — we need per-request logging, redaction rules, and retention controls. can you hook into our SIEM?
[17:07] Jordan: yes logs can be forwarded to your Splunk/Datadog/CloudWatch and we provide request-level audit trails and configurable redaction.

[18:40] Aisha: what's a rough timeline for PoC? we want to prove latency and cost savings compared to our current setup before committing reserved capacity.
[18:47] Jordan: typical PoC is 2–4 weeks: week 1 instrument traffic and baseline, week 2 run benchmarks and tuning, week 3 run a controlled spike and validate SLOs, week 4 finalize findings and pricing. Malik will craft a more detailed plan.

[20:00] Malik: we'll need sample prompts, a few representative sessions, and permission to replay traffic in a staging env. replay at a lower scale is ok.
[20:10] Tom: we can provide two weeks of anonymized traces and a set of 50 canonical prompts.

[21:40] Jordan: one more question on failure modes — if a warm node fails during a spike how does Redwood degrade?
[21:45] Malik: we have multi-tier fallbacks: 1) route to other warm nodes in same pool; 2) if capacity exhausted, fallback to quantized model variant in a cheaper pool; 3) if still saturated, route to hosted API fallback (if allowed) or queue requests with graceful error. you can set policy to prefer latency or prefer success.

[24:00] Aisha: do you support model pinning and gradual rollouts? we need to rollout new fine-tunes with canaries.
[24:05] Malik: yes we support pinning, canary percentages, automatic rollback on quality regression, and A/B rollout policies.

[26:20] Tom: curious: what telemetry do you expose for cost per token and per-route?
[26:25] Jordan: Redwood Console shows token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency percentiles, and tracing hooks. we'll share screenshots in the follow-up.

[28:00] Maria: security question — do you store PII ever? we need to ensure we can enable redaction and never persist sensitive inputs.
[28:08] Malik: you can configure request-level redaction; by default we do not persist user inputs beyond what's required for caching; audit logs can be configured to exclude PII.

[30:10] Jordan: ok to summarize next steps: we'll send the sizing spreadsheet, and Malik will draft PoC plan. Bridgewell will share traffic traces and prompts. schedule SE benchmark the week of June 8. anything else?
[30:22] Aisha: can you also include a short options doc on Dedicated vs Private with pros/cons and estimated cost ranges?
[30:28] Jordan: yes, we'll include that.

[32:00] Ben: small ask — do you have reference customers in healthcare/fintech that did reserved pools?
[32:06] Jordan: yes we'll include anonymized case studies and a short note on regulatory posture.

[33:50] Malik: technical note — if you want extremely fast burst absorb (<1s) the only reliable pattern is over-provisioning warm nodes. otherwise you accept transient p99 bumps while autoscale completes.
[34:05] Tom: right, tradeoffs. we want to size to avoid customer-facing regressions during launches.

[36:30] Aisha: any blockers we should expect for an on-prem path?
[36:36] Malik: on-prem adds network and ops overhead: we need image compatibility, GPU driver matrix, and some manual setup for HSM/KMS. it's doable but typically slower to stand up.

[38:20] Jordan: pricing note — reserved is a commitment; we can structure staged commits to align with your ramp.

[40:00] Maria: timeline-wise, our compliance review cycles are 3 weeks; if PoC is in mid-June we'd aim for procurement decision end of July.
[40:10] Jordan: sounds reasonable.

[41:30] Malik: I'll include measurements to watch during PoC: p95/p99 token latency, cold start times, KV cache hit rate, and cost per 1k tokens.

[43:00] Jordan: final recap: deliverables from Redwood — sizing spreadsheet + ballpark pricing, PoC scope, security/compliance pack. from Bridgewell — traces, prompts, list of regulated tenants. agree to reconvene after Bridgewell uploads traces.
[43:20] Tom: confirmed.
[45:10] Aisha: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[45:20] Jordan: appreciate the time. we'll follow up by email with the artifacts.
[46:30] (call ends)
